oneLineAnswer: A prescription medicine that blocks leukotrienes, chemicals behind asthma and allergy symptoms. It has a boxed warning.
whatItIs: Montelukast is a prescription medicine sold as Singulair and as generics. It belongs to a group called leukotriene receptor antagonists. That means it blocks leukotrienes, which are body chemicals that tighten the airways and drive allergy symptoms. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) first approved it in 1998. It comes as tablets, chewable tablets, and oral granules. PubChem lists its molecular formula as C35H36ClNO3S and a molecular weight near 586.
whatItDoes: It is approved for long-term asthma treatment and asthma prevention in adults and children 1 year and older.
It is also approved to prevent exercise-induced asthma in people 6 years and older.
For hay fever, it is approved to control sneezing, a stuffy or runny nose, and an itchy nose.
US regulators say it should not be a first choice for hay fever.
Many other allergy medicines are widely available and have long safety records.
It is not a rescue medicine. The label says it does not reverse an asthma attack that is already happening.
howPeopleUseIt: It is a widely used medicine.
In 2018, about 9.3 million US patients filled a montelukast prescription at retail pharmacies.
About 2.3 million of those patients were children younger than 17.
The label describes it as a once-daily medicine for asthma, taken in the evening.
For exercise-related breathing problems, the label describes a single dose before exercise rather than an extra daily dose.
It is sold as tablets, chewable tablets, and oral granules.
Some people are prescribed it after other allergy medicines did not work well enough or caused problems.

commonSideEffects: Headache is the most frequently reported effect, but trial rates were nearly the same as placebo.
Sore throat, cough, runny nose, and sinus infection.
Stomach pain, indigestion, diarrhea, and dental pain.
Fever, flu-like illness, and upper respiratory infection.
Mild rises in liver enzymes showed up on blood tests in trials, at rates close to placebo.
seriousSigns: Mood and behavior changes are the main serious concern.
The US label carries a boxed warning about them.
Reported events include agitation, aggression, hostility, depression, anxiety, and sleep problems.
Suicidal thoughts and behavior, including suicide, have been reported.
Other reported events include hallucinations, confusion, bad or vivid dreams, memory problems, restlessness, sleepwalking, stuttering, tremor, and uncontrolled muscle movements.
These events have been reported in people with and without any previous mental health history.
The label and the FDA notice say patients should stop the medicine and contact a clinician if these appear.
Some people reported mood or behavior symptoms only after stopping the medicine, and some symptoms lasted after stopping.
Rarely, serious allergic reactions including anaphylaxis have been reported.
Rare liver injury has been reported, including cholestatic hepatitis, where bile flow is blocked, and other liver-inflammation patterns.
A rare condition with high eosinophils, a type of white blood cell, and blood-vessel inflammation has been reported.
whoShouldAvoid: Anyone allergic to any ingredient in the product. This is the label's only listed contraindication.
People with phenylketonuria (PKU), who cannot process phenylalanine, because two chewable strengths contain it.
For hay fever, regulators reserve it for people who cannot tolerate or are not helped by other allergy medicines.
People with aspirin sensitivity should keep avoiding aspirin and similar anti-inflammatory drugs while taking it.

interactions: The label says no dose adjustment is needed with theophylline, prednisone, oral contraceptives, warfarin, digoxin, and gemfibrozil.
It also covers itraconazole, thyroid hormones, benzodiazepines, decongestants, and anti-inflammatory drugs.
It also lists cytochrome P450 enzyme inducers, drugs that speed up liver breakdown, as needing no dose adjustment.
The label says people with aspirin sensitivity should keep avoiding aspirin and similar drugs.
Montelukast has not been shown to block that reaction.
pregnancyAndChildren: Published studies of pregnant women have not established a link between montelukast and major birth defects. The label notes those studies had limits, such as small size and inconsistent comparison groups. Montelukast passes into human breast milk. The label says available data do not suggest a significant risk to a breastfed infant. In children, safety and effectiveness are not established below 12 months for asthma. The same is true below 6 months for year-round allergies and below 6 years for exercise-related breathing problems. A 56-week study in children aged 6 to 8 found growth rates were similar on montelukast and placebo.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Why montelukast causes mood and behavior effects is not well understood.
Animal studies show the drug reaches the brain in rats, which may be relevant but does not explain the symptoms.
Researchers cannot identify who is most at risk or say how likely these effects are.
A large FDA study found no higher rate of mental health side effects than inhaled corticosteroids.
That study had limits, including relying on health billing records.
Reported cases are voluntary, so the true frequency of rare events such as liver injury cannot be reliably estimated.
It is unclear why some people develop symptoms after stopping the medicine.
No fetched source compared montelukast directly against other allergy medicines for how well it works in everyday use.

gaps: NCCIH has no montelukast page. The URL https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/montelukast returned a 404, so NCCIH is not cited.
The LiverTox entry for montelukast on the NCBI Bookshelf (NBK548264) was attempted but the page served a browser check instead of content, so it could not be fetched and is not cited.
ClinicalTrials.gov was queried and returned studies, but no fetched trial record gave a simple usable claim about what montelukast does, so it is not cited.
MedlinePlus drug monographs were not fetched or used. NLM states they are American Society of Health-System Pharmacists content and copyrighted.
Copyrighted sources named in the brief (Examine.com, Labdoor, MSKCC About Herbs, ConsumerLab, WebMD, Healthline, Drugs.com, RxList) were not fetched, cited, or used.
No numeric dose information is included by design, so the record does not cover how much any age group is directed to take.
DailyMed hosts several montelukast labels that differ by manufacturer and revision date; only one was fetched in full.
summary: This record covers montelukast's approved uses, its boxed warning for mood and behavior effects, other side effects, and the questions the evidence still cannot settle.
